newsitem.title: USA: TWA seen facing difficult talks with pilots.
newsitem.headline: TWA seen facing difficult talks with pilots.

text.p: Trans World Airlines Inc is approaching contract talks with its pilots at a time when record profits at other U.S. airlines have allowed wage increases that TWA cannot afford to match.
"There's not much that TWA can give when the company isn't making any money," said Stephen Klein, an airline analyst with Standard & Poor's Equity Group. TWA lost $71.6 million in the first quarter.

"We would expect TWA's pilot compensation to eventually close the gap with the industry. But future pilot pay raises have to be premised on a return to profitability, which has so far uniquely eluded TWA," said Samuel Buttrick, an analyst with PaineWebber.
TWA, the seventh-largest U.S. airline, is struggling with a dwindling cash supply, the aftermath of last year's crash of Flight 800, recent management turnover and an ageing fleet.
The St. Louis-based carrier now faces a fresh set of hurdles as labor contracts with its pilots, machinists and flight attendants become amendable later this year.

The pilots union said it would send a letter to TWA Chairman Gerald Gitner next week, asking to amend certain sections of the labor contract. The two sides would then have to met within 30 days to exchange opening proposals for a new labor contract. The current contract, which started September 1, 1994, becomes amendable on August 30.

"We will be seeking nothing less than returning the TWA pilots to a contract comparable to those of our brothers and sisters at United, Delta, Northwest, USAir and others. That includes pay rates, work rules and benefits," Don Jacobs, chairman of the pilots' master executive council, said in a recorded message to the union members.

The union declined to provide specific pay goals but said TWA pilots make about 40 percent less than pilots at rival airlines. The pilots said they are seeking paybacks for concessions made to help the airline through two bankruptcy reorganizations.

"As we clearly understand our company's situation, so must the management understand that the TWA pilots mean to achieve a return on our investment. We have invested over $1 billion to secure a future in terms of job security and future retirement benefits," Jacobs said.

Although TWA's employees have made concessions, workers also gained an estimated 13 percent ownership stake as part of the 1992-93 bankruptcy reorganization. TWA underwent a second bankruptcy reorganization in 1995.
TWA said it would to begin early contract negotiations with the pilots, but declined further comment.
"We will negotiate at the negotiating table. We have agreed to an early start of negotiations," TWA spokesman Mark Abels said.

The pilots at TWA will face a more difficult and extended battle than those waged at rival airlines that posted record profits, such as AMR Corp's American Airlines and UAL Corp's United Airlines, industry experts said.
TWA stands on much weaker financial ground than its rivals, and TWA employees have already made significant concessions, which limits both sides' ability to negotiate, labor experts said.

"TWA workers have made sacrifices in years past and may be looking for parity to other airlines, but it's an apples-to-oranges comparison to compare them to other airlines," said Joseph Blasi, a professor at Rutgers University's School of Management and Labor Relations.

TWA posted a first-quarter loss of $71.6 million, or $1.54 a share, on revenues of $762.3 million. The results beat analysts' expectations of a loss of $1.61, but exceeded the airline's 1996 first-quarter loss of $1.46.

TWA also has been late in making payments to some airports and its cash supply has slipped to about $136.5 million at the end of the March quarter from $181.6 million at the end of December. TWA's auditors have raised questions about the airline's ability to continue as a "going concern."
TWA is often cited as the "last fixer-upper" in the U.S. airline industry. Some analysts have questioned whether TWA can revive itself before the next downturn in the industry.

"We've seen a number of airlines come back from bankruptcy or near-bankruptcy, so it's not beyond a possibility that they could turn around," Klein said. "The difference is that TWA may be trying to turn around when the industry is approaching a downturn instead of an upswing," Klein said.

Klein expects the pilots' contract talks to drag on for about two years, with the results being one of three scenarios: the pilots eventually getting raises, getting a larger ownership stake or becoming unemployed.
